questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 3 \\ 1 & 3 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=-2.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that we are given a $3\times 3$ matrix with the following eigenvalues:

- $\lambda =4$ of algebraic multiplicity $2$

- $\lambda =-2$ of algebraic multiplicity $1$

As a result, we have one $1\times 1$ Jordan block ${J}_{1}(-2)$ corresponding to $\lambda =-2.$
However, there are two possibilities for the Jordan blocks corresponding to $\lambda =4:$

- *Case I.* We may get the single $2\times 2$ Jordan block ${J}_{2}(4).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =4$ form the following chain:

$$
{v}_{2}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }0
$$

- *Case II.* We may get a composition of two $1\times 1$ Jordan blocks, namely ${J}_{1}(4)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(4).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =4$ form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{2}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

To figure out which of the cases we obtain in this situation, let's find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda =4.$

Computing $A-4I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 3 \\ 1 & 3 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -3 & 3 \\ 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -3 & 3 \\ 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+\frac{4}{3}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & -3 & 3 \\ 0 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\text{nullity}(A-4I)=1,$ there will be only one eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =4,$ say, ${v}_{1}.$ So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =4$ form the following chain: 

$$
{v}_{2}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }0
$$

Therefore, we have *case I*, and $A$ has the following Jordan canonical form:

$$
{J}_{2}(4)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(-2)=[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 & 3 \\ -6 & -1 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & -7\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=5,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=-7.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that we are given a $3\times 3$ matrix that has precisely $3$ distinct eigenvalues. 

Therefore, $A$ is diagonalizable, and its Jordan canonical form is

$$
{J}_{1}(5)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(2)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(-7)=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -7\end{aligned}].
$$

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}9 & 2 & -2 \\ -6 & 1 & 6 \\ -2 & -2 & 9\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=7,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=5.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that we are given a $3\times 3$ matrix with the following eigenvalues:

- $\lambda =7$ of algebraic multiplicity $2$

- $\lambda =5$ of algebraic multiplicity $1$

As a result, we have one $1\times 1$ Jordan block ${J}_{1}(5)$ corresponding to $\lambda =5.$
However, there are two possibilities for the Jordan blocks corresponding to $\lambda =7:$

- *Case I.* We may get the single $2\times 2$ Jordan block ${J}_{2}(7).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =7$ form the following chain:

$$
{v}_{2}\overset{A-7I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-7I\,}{\to }0
$$

- *Case II.* We may get a composition of two $1\times 1$ Jordan blocks, namely ${J}_{1}(7)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(7).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =7$ form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\overset{A-7I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{2}\overset{A-7I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

To figure out which of the cases we obtain in this situation, let's find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda =7.$

Computing $A-7I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-7I & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 2 & -2 \\ -6 & 1 & 6 \\ -2 & -2 & 9\end{aligned}]-7[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & -2 \\ -6 & -6 & 6 \\ -2 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A-7I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & -2 \\ -6 & -6 & 6 \\ -2 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\text{nullity}(A-7I)=2,$ there will be two eigenvectors that correspond to the eigenvalue $\lambda =7,$ say, ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}.$ So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =7$ form the following chains: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\overset{A-7I\,}{\to }0 \\ {v}_{2}\overset{A-7I\,}{\to }0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have *case II*, and $A$ has the following Jordan canonical form:

$$
{J}_{1}(7)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(7)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(5)=[\begin{aligned}7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.
